explanations.explanation: I get why you'd think so. Job did go quiet earlier (Job 40:4, 5), and a quiet man usually gets to sit down. But the LORD isn't done with him. He says, “Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me.” (Job 40:7)

That's right. Job did go quiet earlier (Job 40:4, 5), but his silence doesn't end anything. The LORD says, “Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me.” (Job 40:7) So Job isn't off the hook yet. He's being asked to answer.

Yes. The LORD asks, “Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” (Job 40:8) That's the whole question. Would Job put God in the wrong just to come out looking right? It's a big question, so read it slowly.

I see why this one tempts you, because it sounds so gentle. But the verse isn't about comfort at all. The LORD asks, “Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” (Job 40:8) It's about clearing your own name, and nobody's getting a warm blanket here.
Nobody's counting coins in this verse. The LORD asks about justice, and the word is “justify.” He says, “Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” (Job 40:8) It's about who gets to be in the right.

explanations.answer: Look on him and bring him low
explanations.explanation: That's it. The LORD says, “Look on every proud man and humble him; trample the wicked where they stand.” (Job 40:12) Earlier He says to “look on every proud man and bring him low.” (Job 40:11) It's a huge job, and I'd be hiding behind my apron.

explanations.answer: Pray for him and let him go
explanations.explanation: That sounds kind, but it isn't in the LORD's words. The challenge says to “look on every proud man and bring him low.” (Job 40:11) Nothing here mentions praying or letting anyone go.

explanations.answer: Warn him and give him time
explanations.explanation: Patient idea, but it isn't what the LORD says. He tells Job, “Look on every proud man and humble him…” (Job 40:12) Warnings and extra time never come up in these verses.

explanations.answer: That Job's own right hand can save him
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, “Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you.” (Job 40:14) Notice the "then." It comes after the LORD's whole list of challenges: an arm like God's, a voice that thunders, humbling the proud and trampling the wicked. (Job 40:9 to 13) The confession is only on the table if Job could pull all of that off.

explanations.answer: That Job was right all along
explanations.explanation: I can see why that'd be the dream ending. But the LORD never says it. What He says is, “Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you.” (Job 40:14)

explanations.answer: That Job should rule the nations
explanations.explanation: Nice promotion, but it's not in the text. The LORD's words are, “Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you.” (Job 40:14) Nobody's handing out a crown here.
Yes, grass. The LORD says, “He feeds on grass like an ox.” (Job 40:15) His bones are tubes of bronze, and he's out there grazing. That's one calm creature.
Fish aren't on this menu. The verse says Behemoth “…feeds on grass like an ox.” (Job 40:15) Maybe you were thinking ahead to Leviathan, who lives in the sea and comes up next.

A creature this strong, you'd expect a hunter. But the text says he “…feeds on grass like an ox.” (Job 40:15) All that power, and he's out there eating grass. The hills even yield him their produce. (Job 40:20)
That's right. The LORD says of Behemoth, “only his Maker can draw the sword against him.” (Job 40:19) Nobody else is on that list. Not one name.

Samson, one of Israel's judges (Judges 15:20), was known for his great strength (Judges 16:6), so I see the guess. But the verse says, “only his Maker can draw the sword against him.” (Job 40:19) That leaves room for one, and it isn't Samson.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:4), took on Goliath (1 Samuel 17:50), so I see the guess. But the verse says, “only his Maker can draw the sword against him.” (Job 40:19) So even a king doesn't make the list.

The first half is right, but the second half is the catch. The text says, “The hills yield him their produce, while all the beasts of the field play nearby.” (Job 40:20) Play, not run and hide. These animals seem to hang around him just fine.

You caught it. “The hills yield him their produce, while all the beasts of the field play nearby.” (Job 40:20) The beasts play nearby, which is the opposite of running and hiding. The second half of that statement is where it goes wrong.

Yes. “Though the river rages, Behemoth is unafraid; he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth.” (Job 40:23) Raging water doesn't rattle him. The Jordan surges all the way up to his mouth, and he stays secure. I'd be doing laps on my gold base.

This one's the opposite of what the text says. “Though the river rages, Behemoth is unafraid; he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth.” (Job 40:23) The river rages, and he doesn't flinch. Unafraid and secure is the whole point of the verse.
Yes. The LORD asks, “Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare?” (Job 40:24) The question is about catching him. And the question answers itself.
Close, but seeing him isn't the question. The LORD asks, “Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare?” (Job 40:24) He's asking about catching him, not looking at him.

The name is already out there, since the LORD just said it. The last question is, “Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare?” (Job 40:24) It's about catching him, not naming him.

explanations.answer: Whether Job could tame and control him
explanations.explanation: Right. Hooks, cords, leashes, even making him a slave for life. (Job 41:1-5) Every question is about whether Job could bring Leviathan under his control. Question after question, same direction.

explanations.answer: Whether Job has ever seen him up close
explanations.explanation: The questions aren't about what Job has seen. They're about what Job could do: “Can you put a cord through his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook?” (Job 41:2) It's all about taming and controlling.

explanations.answer: Whether Job knows where he lives
explanations.explanation: No address questions here. The LORD asks things like, “Will he make a covenant with you to take him as a slave for life?” (Job 41:4) It's all about whether Job could bring Leviathan under control.
Yes. “If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it!” (Job 41:8) One try is all it takes. Nobody signs up for a second round. That's a lesson you only need once.

I see where that comes from, since the LORD does ask about a covenant just before this. (Job 41:4) But this verse says, “…you will remember the battle and never repeat it!” (Job 41:8) No dealmaking happens here.
Nobody's going anywhere in this verse. It says, “If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it!” (Job 41:8) It's one fight, and you'd remember it.

explanations.answer: Who is able to stand against Me
explanations.explanation: That's the one. “No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me?” (Job 41:10) The LORD goes from the creature straight to Himself. If no one is fierce enough to rouse Leviathan, who could stand against the One who says, “Everything under heaven is Mine.”? (Job 41:11)

explanations.answer: Who is brave enough to hunt him
explanations.explanation: That sounds like the next logical question. But the LORD says, “Then who is able to stand against Me?” (Job 41:10) He turns it from Leviathan to Himself.

explanations.answer: Who will warn the people of the sea
explanations.explanation: The verse never mentions people of the sea. The LORD says, “No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me?” (Job 41:10) The question He asks is who is able to stand against Him.
It's the opposite. The LORD says, “Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine.” (Job 41:11) Nobody has put God in debt. There's no tab.

You've got it. “Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine.” (Job 41:11) God owes nobody, because everything under heaven is already His. The question answers itself.

explanations.answer: So tight no air can pass between them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, that's it. “One scale is so near to another that no air can pass between them.” (Job 41:16) That's armor with no gaps, and no gaps means nothing slips through. The next verse says, “They are joined to one another; they clasp and cannot be separated.” (Job 41:17) Tight and sealed together is the picture.

explanations.answer: Loose enough for water to slip through
explanations.explanation: Picture the reverse. The text says, “One scale is so near to another that no air can pass between them.” (Job 41:16) Loose scales with room to slip through aren't in the text. Tight is the picture.

explanations.answer: Spread apart like feathers on a wing
explanations.explanation: Feathers have gaps, and these scales don't. “One scale is so near to another that no air can pass between them.” (Job 41:16) And “They are joined to one another; they clasp and cannot be separated.” (Job 41:17) The picture is tight and sealed together.

That's right. “Firebrands stream from his mouth; fiery sparks shoot forth!” (Job 41:19) And “Smoke billows from his nostrils…” (Job 41:20) Verse 21 adds, “…flames pour from his mouth.” (Job 41:21) Fire out the mouth and smoke out the nose.

This one's true, though it's hard to believe. “Firebrands stream from his mouth; fiery sparks shoot forth!” (Job 41:19) And “…flames pour from his mouth.” (Job 41:21) The text really does say fire and smoke.

Half right, but the arrow ruins it. “The sword that reaches him has no effect, nor does the spear or dart or arrow.” (Job 41:26) And “No arrow can make him flee…” (Job 41:28) So an arrow does nothing either.

Yes, the statement falls apart at the arrow. “No arrow can make him flee; slingstones become like chaff to him.” (Job 41:28) The sword, the spear, the dart and the arrow have no effect on him. (Job 41:26) So the arrow does nothing to him either.

explanations.answer: Nothing on earth is his equal
explanations.explanation: Yes. “Nothing on earth is his equal—a creature devoid of fear!” (Job 41:33) The LORD says it plainly. Leviathan is one of a kind, and nothing on earth matches him. That's how the LORD sums him up.

explanations.answer: He is the oldest of all creatures
explanations.explanation: The white-haired wake might make you think of age. But the text says it only looks that way: “one would think the deep had white hair!” (Job 41:32) The LORD sums him up with, “Nothing on earth is his equal…” (Job 41:33)

explanations.answer: He is afraid only of the deep
explanations.explanation: Not even that. The LORD calls him “…a creature devoid of fear!” (Job 41:33) The summing up is, “Nothing on earth is his equal…”

That's right. “He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud.” (Job 41:34) Remember the LORD told Job to look on every proud man. (Job 40:12) Here is a creature who already looks down on them all. Leviathan looks down on the very ones the LORD told Job to humble.
Sea makes sense, since he stirs it up like a cauldron. (Job 41:31) But the last line says, “he is king over all the proud.” (Job 41:34) His kingdom is the proud.
Beasts sound natural, but the verse says something else. “He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud.” (Job 41:34) It's the proud he rules. The word isn't beasts, it's proud.

explanations.answer: That God can do all things
explanations.explanation: Yes. Job says, “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted.” (Job 42:2) After all those questions, that's where he begins. Nobody can block God's plans.

Job doesn't say that here, and he's not keeping score for the friends. He says, “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted.” (Job 42:2) Every word of it is about God.
Nothing in these verses says that. Job says, “I know that You can do all things and that no plan of Yours can be thwarted.” (Job 42:2) He's talking about who God is, not about his own pain.
Yes. Job says, “Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.” (Job 42:3) He's quoting the LORD's earlier question first. Then he owns up to it himself.

This one is true, and it's Job himself saying it. “Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know.” (Job 42:3) Those are his own words. He even repeats the LORD's question first, and then he owns up to it.

explanations.answer: Before he'd heard of God but now he's seen Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Job says, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” (Job 42:5) Before, he had heard of God. Now he says he has seen Him. It's like the difference between reading a recipe and smelling the cookies in the oven.

explanations.answer: Before he'd doubted God but now he trusts Him
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a nice turnaround, but Job doesn't say it. He says, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” (Job 42:5) The change is from hearing to seeing.

explanations.answer: Before he'd feared God but now he loves Him
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't put it that way. His words are, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You.” (Job 42:5) It's about hearing versus seeing.
Yes. Job says, “Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.” (Job 42:6) It's a heavy line, and I think it's a heavy moment. Just before it, he says he has seen God. (Job 42:5)
I understand wanting a happier word. But Job says, “Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.” (Job 42:6) It's a heavy line, not a party.
Rest would be nice after that long speech. But Job's last words here are, “Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.” (Job 42:6) The word is repent.
